fields.title: Recognize a Recorded Contribution
fields.content:
The NHCP registry records that Gabriela Silang continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silang. This is a specific contribution by a woman in a named movement. A history that stops with Diego would miss that continuation. Begin with the recorded action rather than guessing what someone could do from gender alone.

The source is a later historical marker, not a complete account of every meeting or participant. Recognizing Gabriela does not prove that all women had the same role, opportunity or experience. Nor does an unnamed woman in a short account automatically mean that women did nothing. Ask which action is recorded and what further evidence would help identify other contributions. You do not need to invent a speech to value a contribution. This lesson examines leadership respectfully; it does not ask classmates to disclose identity or act out a battle.

fields.title: Indigenous Communities Made Decisions
fields.content:
A UCLA summary of research by Stephen Acabado and Marlon Martin describes Ifugao resistance to Spanish conquest alongside strategies that strengthened local organization. This is a named Indigenous case in the northern Philippines. It challenges an account that treats communities only as people acted upon by outsiders, without decisions of their own.

Agency does not mean unlimited freedom or that every choice was made by everyone equally. Ask what decisions the research supports and how conditions affected them. Do not turn one Ifugao case into the identical history of all Indigenous peoples. Communities have different histories, institutions and relationships. The summary draws on archaeological investigation and collaboration; it is not a transcript of every persons thoughts. Our diagram is a modern evidence guide, not a reconstruction of a universal Indigenous council. Keep claims tied to the particular community and evidence.

Open the three clues. Choose a supported explanation. Use Explain for help, then return to this evidence before practice.

fields.title: Contact Was Not the Same as Submission
fields.content:
The Ifugao research summary describes people using colonial economic opportunities to strengthen their organization while resisting Spanish conquest. This lets us examine contact and resistance together. Having an exchange or a connection does not by itself prove that a community gave up all decisions. Isolation and total submission are not the only possibilities to investigate.

Ask separate questions: What connection is recorded? Who made a decision? What evidence shows authority being carried out? A trade connection alone cannot answer all three. The lesson concerns a historical case, not a present-day legal ruling about territory. Nor does autonomy imply that every resident had equal influence or that a community never changed. Avoid treating Indigenous people as frozen in the past. Investigate changing strategies and conditions through evidence, without inventing a particular bargain, council vote or shared motive that the summary does not provide.

fields.title: A Cultural Role Needs Its Own Evidence
fields.content:
CulturEd identifies Tamblot as a babaylan who led an uprising in Bohol in 1621. The account connects the case with earlier religious practices. It supplies an example of cultural leadership in a particular place and period. A cultural role can matter to an account of resistance, alongside other forms of leadership and organization.

Do not use the role label to assign the same gender, beliefs or actions to every person called a babaylan. This lesson does not classify Tamblot as a woman or turn the case into every Indigenous communitys story. The entry acknowledges limited information about his life. A gap is a reason to investigate, not permission to invent dialogue or motives. Studying a religious practice does not require following it or judging a classmates faith. Our cards describe evidence; they are not instructions for rituals or costumes. Later sources and community knowledge may help answer different questions.

fields.title: Study History with Communities
fields.content:
The UCLA research summary emphasizes collaboration with Ifugao communities in studying history and heritage. This matters because a history written only through outside descriptions can miss community knowledge and questions. Archaeological evidence and community participation can help examine earlier interpretations rather than simply repeat them.

For a fictional classroom model, a history team compares a written description, material evidence and a community explanation. Each has a source, context and limits. The model is not an authentic interview or permission to collect sensitive family information. Different evidence should be examined carefully, not ranked by assuming one identity is always right or wrong. A disagreement calls for respectful questions and further investigation. Your journal should identify whose action is supported, whose perspective is included and what remains unknown. A fuller account recognizes contributions without assigning everyone the same experience.
